“Perfection” can mean a first perfection, whose loss removes the thing itself, such as the form that makes a soul what it is, or a second perfection, whose loss leaves the thing in existence, such as knowledge. The first sense is intended here, especially in all but the final clause of the sermon; the final clause may use the second sense. — س قده

The Imam's “sincerity” may have a higher mystical meaning: passing beyond the level where existence is considered with its names and attributes to the hidden oneness beyond all names. The commentator recalls a verse of ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī: “None has made the One one; whoever declares Him one has denied Him.”

In pure spiritual self-effacement, no pointing is possible. As the Imam says in answer to Kumayl's question about reality, it is “the unveiling of the lights of majesty without a pointer.” Even a mental pointer would set a limit, because the pointer would assert its own existence alongside what it points to. — س قده

The word “therefore” seems awkward here. The statement “whoever knows what Necessary Being means” appears to refer to our understanding of a concept, not to direct knowledge of the reality itself. Three readings are possible.

On the first, the opening describes the beginning of knowledge and the later phrase about the reality of existence describes its perfection. But this goes against the plain sense and does not work: the author explicitly says that the first kind of knowledge leads us to affirm that a Necessary Being exists.

On the second reading, both parts concern direct knowledge rather than concepts. The word “knows” can suggest acquaintance with a particular reality, and “meaning” can refer to the reality meant rather than a general idea. This reading makes better sense of “therefore.”

The third, and strongest, reading takes the opening as perfected knowledge through concepts, and the later passage as a step beyond that to direct awareness. The use of “meaning” supports this. Moreover, the author does not say that understanding the meaning of Necessary Being is the same as directly seeing that being. He offers a proof. Someone wholly absorbed in direct awareness would not need a chain of proof in the same way. The proof is quoted from an earlier knower; the later statement is the author's own.

On this third reading, someone first understands the general concept of Necessary Being. When the mind considers existence as such, it finds that one kind of existent does not need to be related to anything else in order to be called existent: that is God. Another kind exists only through its dependence on something else; indeed, its existence is that dependence. Understanding this distinction leads the mind to affirm a Necessary Being, because dependent beings exist and need their source. The author then takes a further step: if knowing the concept can lead to affirming God's existence, how much stronger is direct awareness of existence itself?

An objection remains. Direct awareness normally seems to concern either knowing oneself or knowing something that comes from oneself. God is neither the knower's self nor an effect of the knower. How, then, can one know Him directly? The reply is that one can know through the passing away of one's sense of separate self in what is known. No alien existence need stand between the knower and the reality of existence. What makes them distinct is not utterly foreign to what they share. Forgetfulness creates the distance; the passing away of self-centered awareness removes it.

“Perhaps” may emphasize or qualify the claim. In some essences, identity with knowledge can be explained through a mental form that exists in itself. But self-awareness in the soul or intellect cannot depend on such an essence-concept: the soul may know itself while overlooking every universal concept. — س قده
For created existences, especially immaterial ones, “what is it?” and “why is it?” may have the same answer, as Aristotle observes. — س قده
This concerns complete conceptual knowledge. Direct awareness requires no reflection or deliberation. — س قده

The author does not mean that one cannot form a mental supposition of an impossibility. He means that one cannot understand it coherently. Some impossibilities, such as an effect preceding its cause, can be imagined in a mistaken way; others, such as a thing being denied of itself, cannot be conceived without contradiction.

The presence of a thing includes the reality on which its existence depends. Just as understanding an essence brings its defining parts into view, the existence of an effect brings the source that sustains it into view. — س قده

“Angels and those who have knowledge” can refer together to the higher, separate causes and to all beings capable of knowledge. Another reading takes the angels as the first universal intellects and those who know as universal souls, the later spiritual principles in the order of creation.
The more fully an existent gathers perfections, the fewer its absences and losses, and the greater its simplicity and unity. — س قده
An objection might be made: the author often says that what distinguishes one thing is the same reality through which it agrees with other things. Why does he reject that argument here so sharply?

The answer is that the principle belongs to existence, not to separate essences or the concepts used to define them. In the definition of a kind, the feature that distinguishes it from other kinds is not simply the general nature that it shares with them. The feature and the general nature are distinct in thought. Their existence, however, can be one, especially in a simple being. Here the proposed difference would be between the reality of existence and the mere standing of a concept. That is no more a shared way of being than saying that a limited thing is distinguished from existence by its limiting essence.

Besides, the principle is helpful only if the higher level contains the positive reality of the lower level within itself. If the higher level lacks something that must then be added to it, it would be composed of what it possesses and what it lacks—or of a shared core and an additional part. That is exactly what divine simplicity rules out, as the cited sermon teaches.

We have also seen that real existence is itself will, power, and the other perfections. If a supposed “existence” had to receive those attributes as additions, we would no longer be speaking of real existence without qualification. The comparison between the two would break down. There would be no shared reality on which to base the claim that the same thing both distinguishes and unites them. This is a matter of argument, not merely a choice of words. — س قده
The difference between created things and God does not mean that pure existence is deprived of existence. The difference is in their attributes and limits, not in their being cut off from the source.

The point turns on the difference between “fourth of three” and “third of three.” In the first phrase, the word “fourth” does not mean the same thing as in “fourth of four”; it describes God's presence with three others, not His place as a numerical unit alongside them. Existence is not a number or a part of a number. — س قده

Philosophers use this expression for the forms of things said to be present in God's prior knowledge and care. It resembles their saying that the order of created things corresponds to the divine order. The higher realm is described as wide and great because the forms of all things, bodily and immaterial, are present there as general forms free from matter and its limiting conditions. Their existence is through the all-embracing existence of God.

The author uses the expression for the level of the divine names and attributes. That level is particularly vast, because there the differences of meaning can be as numerous as we please without dividing the underlying reality. It is called the lordly realm because, on one mystical view, the divine names and attributes govern the kinds of things. They are the sources even of the luminous exemplars that the Illuminationists call the lords of the kinds.

On the philosophers' other account, it is called the lordly realm because it belongs to the divine side of reality, in contrast to our created world. Here matter, motion, and separation make things seem independent of one another.

“He is all in His oneness” is a saying of al-Fārābī in his discussion of knowledge. In this setting it means that God's one, simple existence contains the reality of all His names and attributes, without becoming divided or losing its unity. — س قده

“States” and “manifestations” may mean the successive appearances of divine light in the material world, one after another, across past and future days. They may also mean the appearances of this light in each kind of being. Every such kind has its own world, with changes both in its substance and in its outward qualities. The rising of the light for it is, in this sense, a new “day.”

Or the words may mean the real divine names and attributes. The concepts we use are names of those names; the real name is existence itself considered through one of its divine perfections. God is revealed to Himself through His essence, through His names and attributes, and through the places where those attributes appear.

In the level where the names are one, each is present in every other according to its existence. Every reality there contains the meaning of every other. The “days” at that level are not separate earthly days. They are gathered into a single eternal presence containing all times, just as the Qur'an speaks of the divine command as one and as swift as the blink of an eye, or nearer.

This level of the names stands between two extremes: God's undivided oneness and the many possible essences that depend on His names and attributes. It connects possibility with necessity and multiplicity with unity. The gathered disclosure of the names is called mercy at the level of attributes. When God's command “Be” appears through His actions in the ordered and varied world, that is called mercy at the level of acts.

It is the divine names, not created things, that are unmade. The Muʿtazilites held that possible essences were fixed before existence; the author instead says that divine names are many meanings within the one real existence. — س قده

This mistake confuses a concept with what the concept refers to. Saying that God's attributes are identical with His essence means their real existence is one with His essence, not that their meanings and concepts are one.

The author describes God as knowing to show that His knowledge is active and sufficient for things to exist, so it also entails power. For God, power does not mean that an act might or might not occur, as it can for us. God's will is not an additional desire beyond His knowledge; it is His knowledge of the order of existence.

Names can be combined, as in “the Most High and the Great,” “the Knowing and the Aware,” and “the Hearing and the Seeing.” They can also be individual names for particular acts, such as being the creator of Zayd or knowing ʿAmr. — س قده

Examples include “the Holy” as manifested in angels, hearing and sight in animals, misguidance in devils, and gentleness in spirits. The whole world, from the earth to the highest lights, is like a hall of mirrors reflecting the one beautiful reality.

The manifestations of God's names are gathered in Him, just as the names themselves are one in their source. In the vision where opposites are reconciled, every severity contains beauty and every affliction its remedy. The sun's light overpowers the stars without denying that they have light; so God's encompassing mercy includes every name.

If existence were only a concept drawn from things, with no real existence of its own, the attributes would be distinct existents in keeping with their different meanings. To avoid that conclusion, later thinkers made the meanings identical. The author rejects this and holds that existence itself is real. — س قده

The unity of the attributes is the unity of God's existence; the many created forms are the manifestations of those attributes. In spiritual vision, opposing forms are reconciled in God. At a lower level, their unity can be seen in their dependence on the one divine source, as many reflections depend on one mirror.

The “image-like, luminous existence” is not mixed with matter. Weak existence, such as that of matter, is not called knowledge or knower, though the reality of knowledge is not wholly absent from it. — س قده

Material bodies are divided into parts, and their bodily forms are not all present to one another. But someone could consider them as processes of ongoing change in their very nature or as a whole whose parts are gathered in one unity, and on that basis say that knowledge runs through them.

The “thing known” here means the form directly known in knowledge that works through representations. A few lines later the author calls it “a pure, luminous existence of awareness.” His point in this principle is that what is immediately known is the known form, rather than the external thing known only through that form.

He is not yet giving a complete division of everything that can be known, nor distinguishing all the kinds of knowledge. The difference between direct presence and knowledge gained through forms will come later.

So it would be a mistake to object that a material thing known through direct presence can exist for the knower exactly as it exists in itself. Such a thing need not be a pure light, free from matter's limitations and from absence, as the author says of the form considered here. One might reply that God's knowledge of material things strips away the rules that govern matter. But that would not fit the plain point of the present passage.
“Known” is used broadly here, for all four kinds of knowledge. In the earlier passage it meant the intellect's universal object, in contrast to sensory perception.

An objection arises about the features said to accompany a person, such as Zayd, when he is understood intellectually. Are these features general ideas of shape, position, and the like? If so, they do not affect what Zayd is, for the Zayd understood as a universal is simply a human being. A general idea of shape is not an actual bodily shape. Whether we think of that idea together with the human concept makes no difference to its existence. What matters in bodily life is a shape or position actually belonging to matter, not the abstract concept of one.

Or are these features meant as spiritual counterparts of bodily organs? Aristotle's description of the intellectual human being may suggest this. In such a being, the 'hand' is whatever enables action and the 'foot' whatever enables movement. If someone could act through intention alone or cross the earth without walking, that power would serve as a hand or foot in the relevant sense. Philosophers do not regard such spiritual features as obstacles to understanding.

A third possibility is that the body's actual shape, position, and color accompany the knowing soul and what it knows. Yet the soul and its knowledge do not disappear when the body disappears, still less when its position, shape, or color changes. Those features cannot be essential to intellectual knowledge.

The answer is a fourth possibility. The features of material individuals can be included in the intellectual reality to which those individuals belong, but in a higher and unified way. The many particular beings are expressions of one reality. They are, so to speak, the spreading rays of a light or the broad bases of cones whose points meet in a higher source. Their shapes and positions therefore have their grounds in that higher reality, not merely in detached abstract concepts.

The human being understood by the intellect is one simple, immaterial existence. It gathers the truth of every human individual into a more complete unity. Its individuals express that unity within multiplicity. The author accordingly says, in his discussion of the soul, that to understand a human being intellectually is to grasp a human being free from any particular size, place, or position, without leaving out any of its defining powers or members. The intellectual human being has head, face, eyes, stomach, hands, and feet, but all are understood in a way shared by many individuals.

Elsewhere he says that removing every accompanying feature is not a condition of understanding a thing. The intellect can understand a human being with all its features—quantity, quality, place, position, time, shape, and members—so long as these are understood in a general intellectual way. He compares this with divine knowledge of particular things.

He does not mean only that the spiritual meanings of these organs are included in a higher unity. He also means that the many features appearing in individuals have their reality within it, although not as features confined to one particular body. The reference to God's knowledge of particulars makes this clear: not an atom in heaven or earth escapes that knowledge. The author's wider rule is to hold together God's transcendence and the scriptural language describing His closeness, without reducing God to a body. — س قده

The same point can be shown in two ways: if the mind can picture size and shape, they are not barriers to being understood; and if these images are present in the mind, they coexist with the intellect as things it understands.

Any mental image, whether a particular imagined image or a universal idea, remains universal in this respect: it could apply to more than one instance. A mental image taken from one particular thing is still not that thing's particular existence.

The first argument begins from the particular nature of self-awareness: if it were an acquired image, it would be universal. The second begins from presence: if it were acquired, we would refer to ourselves as “it,” not “I.” — ط مد ظله

The conclusion is that the soul has no essence separate from its existence and is not a substance in the sense of a defined kind. The author cites Suhrawardī's description of the soul and what lies above it as pure lights and existences. — س قده
This is another way of stating the second argument, and prepares the reply to the objection that follows.
This answers the preceding objection that the soul is built from universal conceptual parts such as broader kind and difference. — س قده

You might say that it would be more fitting to mention “substance” and “rational,” which are essential features, rather than concepts that apply only as additional qualities. But the answer is that the argument moves from the general to the particular, not from what is essential to what is additional. — س قده

The objection is answered either by saying that if the soul is free of its essence, it is even more free of matter, or by observing that forgetting the concept “immaterial substance” supports the claim that self-awareness is not conceptual. The soul can also be described by many perfections without being composed of them.

The images the soul handles may have universal content, as when thought divides and combines concepts. But because they are present to the soul that works with them, they are also particular, concrete forms. If the soul knew them only through other universal images, those images would be the objects it handled instead. — س قده

The objects meant here are the forms that the soul keeps and works upon, not the bodily organs used to receive them. This is clear from the contrast with the later words about people who have reached perfection. The point to be proved is that the soul is directly aware of its powers of perception and movement, rather than knowing them through an added mental picture. Yet the second, third, and fourth arguments, and much of the first, really show that the soul is directly aware of what those powers receive or produce—the forms through which it perceives. The fifth argument concerns the soul's use of the powers, not its awareness of the organs themselves.

There is a quiet reference here to the principle that the knower and what is known become one. Remember, too, the earlier discussion of power and action: ‘power’ can mean the source of an effect. Heat, for example, makes things less dense, and cold makes them denser. In the same way, these forms are sources through which something becomes known.
The author means that advanced knowers may have a more complete, integrated direct awareness; everyone has simple, immediate awareness of the images in their own mind. — س قده

The argument can be set out as follows. Either we are directly aware of the disruption in the particular part of the body where pain occurs, which is the point to be proved, or we know that disruption through an image of it. If through an image, where is the image? If it is in the same affected part, two images of the same kind would occupy one place. If it belongs to the soul at the level of understanding, it would be a general concept, not this particular pain. If it is present in another power, such as sight, then anyone who had the same image in sight ought to feel the same pain. That does not happen. Looking at an injury may produce distress, fear, or another kind of suffering, but it does not produce the particular pain of the injured part.

An objection remains. Why could one form not belong to the soul in its lower, touching power, or arise in a power associated with it, while the other belongs to the bodily organ itself? They would then be present in different ways rather than two things occupying one place.

The answer is that at the level of touch the soul is precisely the touching power. That power works by spreading through and receiving impressions in the body. A form present in it is therefore present in the affected organ as well. The difficulty returns.

Someone might object that knowledge requires the known form to be separated from matter. But that condition applies to knowledge obtained through a mental form, not to direct awareness of a thing through its own presence. The Illuminationists likewise hold that material bodies are directly present to the Light of Lights.

Why, then, can we not know every bodily object directly, without lifting it into a mental form? Because direct awareness occurs when a thing is present to itself or when it is aware of what depends on it as its effect. Other physical things are neither ourselves nor effects produced by us. Our bodily powers and their conditions, however, belong to us in that intimate way. — س قده

The editor qualifies the claim: ordinary sensory pain is generally perceived through an image of a harmful quality in the organ. Because the soul is united with the organ, it also directly experiences that quality. Sensory perception can err and unfolds over time, so it is not simply presence-based knowledge. — ط مد ظله
This means the distress added by imagination when it joins frightening or painful ideas to a sensation, making the suffering worse. — ط مد ظله

The argument also avoids requiring the soul to bring an endless series of images into awareness at once. The earlier argument and this one share the same problem: each added image would itself need to be perceived.
The regress is impossible because it would require an endless chain of similar images, and because it conflicts with our direct experience. — س قده

The deeper problem is the infinite regress of one image being known through another. A mere collection of similar mental images would not be impossible, since mental images do not have the external effects of physical things. — ط مد ظله

The argument is called “from the Throne” because it addresses what makes an act voluntary. It also relies on the idea that knowledge of the powers and love for them are contained in the soul's knowledge and love of itself. This is why the soul can bring its powers into activity through its own presence. — س قده

“Then” marks an order of concepts, not a time sequence. Knowledge of the soul's powers may be contained in its self-knowledge, or be considered as knowledge of its distinct powers; either way, it does not come later in time.

“Concept” here means acquired knowledge, since the distinction between concepts and judgments applies to acquired knowledge. The soul uses its powers through an innate inclination that is already present to it, not through prior deliberation. — س قده
The evidence may show only that we fail to notice our awareness, not that the image itself is absent from awareness. — ط مد ظله

The three kinds of absence may be: the object does not exist; it exists but has no perceptive or luminous form; or it has such a form but that form is not present to this particular power. The wording is compressed, and the examples can be divided in more than one way.

Two things can be distinct only in meaning, as in a knower's awareness of itself, or distinct in existence as well, as in knowing something else. The latter connection may be causal, receptive, or descriptive.

The philosophers of Aristotle’s school confine direct awareness to knowing oneself and deny it in knowing anything else. They therefore treat God's knowledge of possible things as mental images and, in the author's view, deny the fullest kind of knowledge. — س قده

The commentator connects this claim to the author's view that even acquired knowledge is grounded in immaterial forms. Particular images belong to an imaginal world, and universal ideas to intellectual realities; both can have effects in their own order. Their distance from us is what makes them seem universal or indistinct. — ط مد ظله

The “lights” mentioned here are the higher principles of the material kinds of things. They give those kinds their standing, much as the soul sustains the body through its presence. They are also the fullness of those things: not merely the ideas by which we describe them, but the realities from which their existence comes and toward which it is directed. A thing's full reality must be united with it in some way. Otherwise it could not be its completion or its goal.

The point is to prevent a misunderstanding. The author has said that material things, taken in themselves, cannot be direct objects of knowledge. Someone might conclude that the higher principles therefore do not know them. But the higher lights are directly present to themselves and are the complete realities of the material things that depend on them. To have those complete realities present is also to have their less complete forms present. This is not how an image in our mind relates to the thing pictured. Our image neither causes the thing to exist nor joins it in that close relation between many things and their single source. A mental image therefore gives us a weaker knowledge of its object. Even so, the thing is disclosed through the image, just as what we see indirectly is disclosed through the visible form immediately before sight. Nothing need be left out of that disclosure, but it is still not the same kind of knowledge as the higher presence. We can also understand the higher lights more broadly, as including material things within their own sources in a fuller and simpler way.

I would go further. Material things are dark and not directly intelligible to us. In relation to the higher principles, and especially to the First Principle, they are directly known. This is knowledge through presence and action, even if it is not the same as God's knowledge of Himself. A material thing's presence in matter prevents us from grasping it fully, since our awareness does not surround matter and all it contains. But the One who encompasses matter knows it through that very presence. Indeed, the thing is present to the cause that necessarily produces it more fully than it is present to the matter that receives it. Even the thing's presence in its receiver falls within the knowledge of that cause.

The divisions, absences, and passing away that keep us from direct awareness do not limit the Principle that encompasses everything. It is present in what has passed, what is present, and what is yet to come. It remains constant through all things that change and disappear. In relation to that all-embracing presence, separation does not mean exclusion, absence does not mean ignorance, passing away does not mean loss, and darkness does not hide what is there. A prayer says that no dark night, stormy sea, or enclosed darkness conceals anything from God: for Him, darkness itself is light.

Existence, moreover, is what is most fundamental in everything. The way one existence differs from another does not set it outside the reality they share. So the material things need not first be stripped of matter before they can in any sense know their principles. The Qur'an says that nothing exists without praising God. Their knowledge is simple rather than the combined, reflective knowledge we ordinarily call thinking.

There are, then, two senses of life. In the narrower sense, a living being can perceive and act: touch is the lowest kind of perception, and movement by choice is the lowest kind of action. This belongs to animals and higher beings. In the wider sense, life accompanies existence itself and, in truth, is one with it. Knowledge can likewise mean the special awareness that belongs to living creatures, or the deeper knowledge that accompanies existence wherever it is found. With this distinction, we can understand how the author denies that material things are themselves knowledge in one sense while still holding that existence and knowledge are inseparable in another. — س قده

Someone may object that everything, even an immaterial intellect, exists through another—namely God. All things depend on Him so completely that their existence in themselves is also their existence through Him. Would the argument then imply that nothing except God can know itself? No. ‘Existing for another’ here means existing in another as in a material subject. ‘Another’ means matter in the broad sense, including underlying matter and the subject in which a quality exists. The eye, for example, does not see itself merely because it is a power present in a bodily subject. Its dependence on the soul is a different matter. A second objection is that Sadra elsewhere holds sight, hearing, and the other powers to be immaterial.

Should they not therefore know themselves? The principles quoted here are those of the earlier philosophers, whom Sadra follows at the beginning of the inquiry but not at its end. They treated these powers as lodged in matter. Even in Sadra's account, the powers depend strongly on bodily expressions; for this reason their perception requires the presence of matter or something like it. They are not immaterial in the complete way that intellect is. Still, someone who holds that a wholly immaterial sensible form would itself be sensing, sensed, and the act of sensing can also hold that a sensory power freed from gross matter knows itself at its own level.

Its sensing belongs to the soul, since the soul gathers all its powers; the object sensed is the form disclosed by that power. The power makes the soul manifest, and the perceived form is the power's own disclosure.
The commentator corrects the claim that the philosophers used a faulty argument. They did not reach the conclusion by combining the two claims above; they established each direction separately.
“Can be understood” includes even a very general way of being understood, such as being known as existent, necessary, or possible. — س قده

The argument runs as follows. If a being free from matter were understood by something else, it would exist for that other knower. It would then seem to depend on something else as a subject in which it was present, contrary to the assumption that it was wholly free from matter.

An objection: why must knowing it place it inside the other being? Could it not be known directly through presence? The answer is that this proof belongs to the philosophers in Aristotle’s school, who treat another being's understanding as the reception of its form. On their account the thing understood in itself must have the same existence as the thing present to its knower. Its very being would then be received in the other, which is the difficulty the proof exposes.

A second objection: universal forms are present in our intellects and are called immaterial. Does this not show that an immaterial form can exist in a subject? Here the word 'immaterial' is being used in different senses. For those philosophers, a universal form is free from external matter and its bodily features, but it is still received in the soul as its subject. On the author's own view, understanding happens through the soul's encounter with the higher realities of kinds, or through union with them. It is not the reception of an image in a subject.

But then, the objector continues, must a universal form know itself? That sounds absurd if we think of the concept of a horse. The reply is that a concept and its intellectual existence are not the same thing. The author does not say that the meaning 'horse' becomes a thinking person. He says that its luminous intellectual existence is united with the knowing intellect. At that level it is intellect and soul, and its existence is aware of itself.

Another proposed proof appeals to a pair of related terms: knower and known. If a separate being is known in its own right, perhaps it must also know in its own right, because the two relations stand on the same level. The author has used an argument like this elsewhere to explain the union of intellect and what it understands. But the commentator doubts that the relation alone proves union. Cause and effect are also related, as are mover and moved. Their relations require them to stand in a corresponding order; they do not require them to be one being. If every related pair were one and the same, we would collapse opposites into a single subject in the same respect.

Nor does saying that the known is 'known in relation to a knower' solve the difficulty. The concepts 'known' and 'knower' remain different. Their difference does not by itself prove that two existences are involved, but their connection does not by itself prove that there is only one. A further argument is needed. One possible approach is to understand the relation as an actual connection of presence and illumination, not merely as a comparison between two concepts. This would explain a kind of union in disclosure without reducing a higher being to a lower one.

To be fair, this is probably the author's real intention. He is not relying on related words alone. His deeper point is that a directly understood, luminous reality has no existence or activity apart from its being disclosed. Even if we supposed that nothing else existed, its own existence would still be a form of understanding. With no other object present, that understanding would be understanding of itself. This differs from an effect, which cannot remain an effect if its cause is removed from consideration. A being known in itself does not require another knower in that way. In actual understanding, moreover, something known in actuality requires an intellect knowing in actuality. That is the proper force of the relation between them. — س قده

“Essence” here means individual existence, not a universal definition. In God, knowledge and every other perfection are His existence, since He has no defined essence apart from existence. In other separate beings, their perfections are identical with their existence, not with the concepts used to describe their kind.
